newsitem.title: USA: Change suggested for shareholder proposal rule - SEC. [CORRECTED 18:51 GMT]
newsitem.headline: Change suggested for shareholder proposal rule - SEC. [CORRECTED 18:51 GMT]

text.p: Securities and Exchange Commission commissioner Steven Wallman suggested changes to shareholder proposal rules to make them less subjective in a speech to an institutional investors conference here Tuesday.
In prepared remarks, Wallman said "the current system has two problems -- the lack of a guiding principle, and heavy reliance on subjective line drawing."

Wallman said the most substantive suggestion would allow shareholder proposals that related to certain legal rights and obligations, or core proposals, and those with support of three percent of outstanding shares.
Under such a revision "almost all traditional corporate governance proposals would be includable under this provision," he said.

He also suggested removing language that used subjective line drawing, clarifying the rules regarding personal grievance proposals, raising resubmission thresholds for shareholder proposals, and allowing frivolous proposals to be excluded per se.
Proposals that were neither core or frivolous would be includable subject to a lottery, with a minimum and three and a maximum of six allowed depending on the size of the company.
Finally, rule changes would allow companies discretionary authority over "late resolutions."

Wallman said an example of line drawing was the Cracker Barrel position of the SEC, in which a shareholder proposal requesting the board of Cracker Barrel Old Country Store Inc to implement an anti-discrimantory hiring policy was not allowed (corrects from "was allowed"). Such proposals had traditionally been excluded, but exceptions had been made when the proposal was on "social policy concerns."
The ruling was appealed, but the SEC's position was sustained, Wallman said.
Wallman also noted how new technology, and in particular, the internet, was changing the relationship between shareholders and corporations.
"We need to be cognizant of the dangers and protect reasonably against them, but we also need to allow innovation to flourish," he said.
